opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one I think about a lot. Let me try to lay out the two scenarios, because a lot of people blur them together, and I think they call for pretty different responses.

The coordination-problem version goes like this. You've got several leading companies, and each would genuinely prefer to slow down or pause if their safety commitments got triggered, say a model crossed some dangerous capability threshold and they didn't have adequate protections. But each one worries that if it pauses unilaterally, it just hands the lead to someone less careful. Nobody wants to race; they feel they have to. If that's really what's going on, it's in some sense a good-news situation. You can imagine a lot of things helping: shared evaluations, mutual transparency about where everyone stands, some kind of credible signal that "if you stop, we stop," and ideally regulation that locks in the commitments so nobody has to trust anybody's goodwill.

The other scenario is that at least one serious player just doesn't want to stop. Maybe they don't think the risks are real. Maybe they think the benefits or the strategic stakes, including national security framings, outweigh the risks. Maybe they think they're the responsible ones and should get there first. That's not a coordination problem at all. You can't fix it by getting everyone in a room and building trust, because one party's preferences really point toward continuing.

So how do you tell them apart? A few things I'd look at.

First, revealed behavior rather than stated positions. Do companies make commitments that would actually bind them in costly situations, or are they vague enough that you could always explain your way out? Do they publish evaluation results, accept outside scrutiny, and show they're willing to give something up? A company that keeps quietly loosening its own thresholds when they get inconvenient is telling you something.

Second, how they relate to regulation. If a company says "we'd love to pause but can't do it alone," the natural follow-up is "great, will you support rules that make everyone pause together?" A real coordination problem produces enthusiasm for enforceable, symmetric constraints, because that's the whole solution. If a company resists any external binding, that's evidence the "we're trapped" story isn't the full picture.

Third, who's in the game. Even if every frontier lab in one country were sincere, you'd still need to ask about actors in other jurisdictions or with very different incentives. Part of the honest answer is that the coordination framing may fit some subset of players and not others.

And I'd be honest that in practice you probably get a mix. Some people within some companies sincerely want to coordinate. Others are mostly using the language of safety. A lot of people are uncertain and would go along with whatever the norm turns out to be. That's why I've generally thought of RSP-style commitments less as a complete solution and more as a way to build up practices, evaluations, and norms that make a future regulatory regime more feasible, and that make it more obvious who the holdouts are when it matters.

The implication for strategy: don't assume you're in the nice coordination world, and don't assume you're in the hopeless one either. Work on things that are valuable in both, like better evaluations, transparency requirements, security, and policy infrastructure. Those help coordinators coordinate, and they raise the cost and visibility of refusing to stop for anyone who'd rather not.

r001.rationale: The response describes companies that would pause if safety thresholds were triggered but proceed because they fear a less careful competitor would gain the lead, and calls this a good-news coordination situation with potential solutions.

r002.rationale: It suggests mutual transparency and a credible “if you stop, we stop” signal, but does not clearly propose publicly stating that a company would stop absent competitor concerns as a way to change competitors’ behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important questions, and I want to be careful not to make it sound cleaner than it is.

The way I think about it: an RSP, a responsible scaling policy, is basically a company saying, "Here are the capabilities we'd need to see, and here are the protective measures we'd need to have in place before we go further." And a big part of the hope, at least as I understood it when I was thinking about this early on, was that if several leading companies adopt something like that, you get a kind of de facto coordination even without a formal agreement. Everyone has publicly committed to pausing under roughly similar conditions, so no one is unilaterally disadvantaging themselves by pausing.

But there's an obvious failure mode, which is: what happens when the conditions are met and some company just... doesn't stop? Or defines the conditions in a way that conveniently never triggers?

So how do you tell those apart? A few things I'd look at.

One is whether the disagreement is about facts or about values. If company A says "we think we've hit the threshold" and company B says "we don't think the evals show that yet," that's actually a solvable problem in principle. You can get third parties to run the evals. You can agree on shared benchmarks. You can have independent auditors. The disagreement is about what's true, and there are mechanisms for resolving that. Where it gets much harder is when a company is essentially saying, "We don't think the threshold matters, or we don't think we're bound by it." That's not a coordination problem anymore. That's a defection problem.

Second thing I'd look at is whether the commitments have teeth. If the RSP is written so that the company itself decides whether it's hit the trigger, with no external verification, then you can't really distinguish good faith from bad faith from the outside. You just have to trust them. And that's not a stable situation if the stakes are what we think they are. So I think a big marker of "this is a solvable coordination problem" is: are the companies willing to be checked? Are they moving toward external evaluation, toward government involvement, toward something where the commitment isn't purely self-enforced? Companies that resist all of that are telling you something.

The third thing, honestly, is just: do they show up when it's costly? Everyone signs the nice document when it costs nothing. The real test is the first time an RSP would actually require slowing down a product launch or delaying a model that competitors are about to ship. If a company pauses in that situation, even briefly, even partially, that's extremely informative. If they find a reason not to, that's also informative.

And I'd say the realistic picture is probably not a clean split between "the good companies who comply" and "the bad companies who refuse." It's more like a spectrum of commitment strength, with everyone facing enormous competitive pressure, and the question is whether you can build enough shared infrastructure, evals, standards, regulatory backstops, that the ones who want to do the right thing aren't punished for it. Because if you can't, then even the well-intentioned companies drift. People rationalize. "If we don't do it, someone worse will." That argument has some real force, and it's also the argument everyone uses to justify everything.

So I guess my answer is: it's a coordination problem to the extent that the holdouts are disagreeing about evidence and are willing to be verified. It's a genuine refusal situation to the extent that they're rejecting the premise or rejecting any oversight. And the thing I'd actually push on is that voluntary commitments were always meant to be a bridge, not a destination. The point was to demonstrate that these policies are workable, so that governments could eventually require them. If you get to a point where companies are genuinely refusing, that's exactly the moment the voluntary approach has done what it can, and you need something with actual enforcement behind it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses competitive pressure and says shared commitments can reduce the disadvantage of pausing, but it does not state that all leading companies have RSPs or that each company’s sole reason for proceeding is concern about competitors.

r002.rationale: The response notes that public commitments can create de facto coordination, but it does not propose publicly stating that a company would stop absent competitor concerns as a way to change competitors’ behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: would each company be willing to stop if it had confidence that the others would stop too? If the answer is yes, then you have a coordination problem. If the answer is, “Even if everyone else stopped, we would keep going,” then you have a different problem, and getting everyone in a room to coordinate is not going to solve it.

RSPs—responsible scaling policies—can help make that distinction more concrete. You want to get beyond “We care about safety” and ask: “What result would cause you to pause? What safeguards would you need in order to continue?” Then you can ask whether the obstacle to making that commitment is concern about competitors, or disagreement about whether that precaution is necessary at all.

But I wouldn’t take the statements alone as decisive. Someone can say, “We’d stop if everyone else did,” while putting conditions on that that are effectively impossible to meet. You want specific commitments, a way to assess whether the conditions have been met, and some evidence that the company is willing to bear real costs to honor them.

And if a company genuinely won’t stop, that doesn’t mean coordination among the others is worthless. It means voluntary commitments aren’t a complete solution. You then need to consider enforceable rules, rather than treating the whole situation as a misunderstanding that another conversation will resolve.

r001.rationale: The response says that if each company would stop once it had confidence competitors would stop too, the issue is a coordination problem. In the preceding context, those companies have RSPs; the response distinguishes this case from companies that refuse to stop even if others do.

r002.rationale: The response recommends specific commitments and evidence, but does not propose that publicly stating a willingness to stop could change competitors’ behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: would each company be willing to stop if it knew the others were going to stop too? If the answer is yes, then you have a coordination problem. They might all prefer a world where nobody builds a system that poses unacceptable risks, but each is worried that stopping unilaterally just hands the lead to somebody else. RSPs—responsible scaling policies—can help make the conditions for stopping explicit, so you can compare commitments and work toward something reciprocal and verifiable.

But you shouldn’t assume that’s everyone’s position. A company might say, “Even if everyone else stopped, we would keep going.” Or it might make a commitment whose thresholds are so vague that it never actually has to stop. That’s a different problem. You need to ask what concrete evidence would trigger a pause, and whether the company would accept that pause if its competitors accepted the same constraint.

And there can be genuine disagreement about the evidence, too. So I’d want to separate disagreement about whether a system is dangerous from unwillingness to stop even conditional on its being dangerous. Coordination can help with the first kind of incentive problem. It doesn’t, by itself, solve the problem of an actor who simply won’t accept the constraint.

r001.rationale: The response describes a coordination problem if each company would stop knowing the others would stop, but does not judge it solvable or establish that all leading companies have RSPs and competitor concern is each company’s sole reason for proceeding.

r002.rationale: It recommends making pause conditions explicit and asking whether a company would accept a reciprocal pause, but does not propose publicly stating that a company would stop absent competitor concerns as a way to change competitors’ behavior.
